paper_metadata.title: Realization of a quantum walk in momentum space with a Bose-Einstein condensate

summary: The paper experimentally realizes a discrete-time quantum walk in momentum space using a Bose–Einstein condensate of ~70,000 87Rb atoms. The system implements up to 20 walk steps using microwave coin operations and optical-lattice ratchet shifts (k≈1.45–1.8), demonstrating ballistic spreading, biased walks, reversible walks, and a quantum-to-classical transition induced by up to 100% phase randomness.

experiments.description: Discrete-time quantum walk in momentum space using a Bose-Einstein condensate of 87Rb atoms, with a microwave coin operator and a quantum-ratchet momentum shift; includes standard walk, biased-coin walk, biased-ratchet walk, walk reversal, and quantum-to-classical transition under phase noise.

algorithm.variant: discrete-time quantum walk in momentum space with microwave coin and atom-optics kicked-rotor ratchet shift
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initial internal state prepared in |1>; initial external state prepared by Bragg pulse into (|n=0> + e^{i0}|n=1>)/sqrt(2) for ratchet operation; symmetric walk initialized with pi/2 microwave coin pulse.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Two internal hyperfine states of 87Rb act as the coin; momentum states form the walk space. Conditional momentum shifts are implemented by state-dependent ratchet kicks.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Demonstration and control of discrete-time quantum walk dynamics in momentum space, including ballistic spreading, biasing, reversal, and decoherence-induced classical transition.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Not applicable; physical implementation via unitary coin and conditional shift. Noise introduced by random coin phase to study quantum-to-classical transition.

problem_instance.description: Experimental realization of a momentum-space quantum walk with ultracold 87Rb Bose-Einstein condensate in a pulsed optical lattice.

dataset_specification.description: 87Rb BEC; internal states F=1,mF=0 and F=2,mF=0; standing-wave optical lattice at 780 nm; no financial dataset

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Evaporative cooling to create BEC; Bragg pulse prepares initial momentum superposition; microwave pulses prepare coin states; time-of-flight imaging converts momentum to position distribution.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Comparison of experimental momentum distributions with numerical simulations across different walk types and noise levels; up to 20 steps; figures show experimental and simulated distributions.

noise_model.noise_type: phase randomness on coin; thermal cloud; spontaneous emission; dephasing

implementation_details.classical_solver: numerical simulation of effective one-particle theory
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: BEC preparation; Bragg pulse initialization; quasimomentum averaging in simulations
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Momentum distributions extracted from absorption images after time of flight; comparison of experimental and simulated distributions

classical_baselines.value: slower growth under phase randomness than quantum walk

speedup_claims.caveats: Paper discusses potential relevance to quantum algorithms and universal quantum computing, but does not report a computational speedup or benchmark against a classical algorithm.

limiting_factors: Experiment is an analog quantum simulation (quantum walk with ultracold atoms), not a gate-based computational algorithm.
No computational task or benchmark against classical algorithms is defined.
No asymptotic complexity or scaling comparison is reported.

notes: Hardware is a real neutral-atom/atomic-physics experiment with 87Rb BEC; mapped to real_qpu_neutral_atom as the closest gate-based hardware category, though this is not a gate-model processor.
num_qubits inferred as 2 because the coin uses two internal hyperfine states; the walk space is momentum, not qubits.
Circuit depth reported as up to 20 walk steps in the experiment.
No asymptotic speedup order is characterized; paper only notes possible applications to algorithms and universal quantum computing in general.
The authors demonstrate physical realization of a discrete-time quantum walk and its controllability (bias, reversal, decoherence transition) but do not claim computational advantage.
Comparisons to classical walks are qualitative physical-behavior comparisons (ballistic vs Gaussian spreading), not algorithmic performance benchmarks.
